2. The appellants filed the above suit for declaration of their title and recovery of khas possession in 6.21 acres of land as detailed in the schedules to the plaint. 

 3. The plaintiffs' case is that Madhu Mondal and Haran Mondal had raiyati interest in the suit land under the landlord Chatterjee Babu at the rent of Tk. 50.00 as recorded in khatian 243 of the suit mouza. The further case of the plaintiffs is that Haran Mondal and Madhu Mondal surrendered the holding in favour of the landlord and Madhu Mondal and Takim Mondal took fresh lease of the suit lands at Tk. 22 and 1/2 , each by executing two different kabuliats dated 17.2.40 Vide Ext. 1 and 1(a) in favour of the landlords. They possessed the land accordingly. Takim Mondal settled the kha schedule land with one Paran Mondal at a rent of Tk. 9.00. Subsequently, Madhu and Takim again surrendered their tenancies orally in favour of the landlords and the landlords entered into khas possession of the land. Subsequently, the interests of Chatterjce Babu were auction purchased by one Satyen Babu in auction for arrear of rent in Rent Execution Case No. 1722/44. The auction purchaser took sale certificate and delivery of possession in land though Court and possessed the same. He then sold the land to one Ramani Sundari by a registered kabala dated 9th Bhadra, 1359 BS. Subsequently, Ramanj Sundari sold the suit land to the plaintiffs by registered kabala dated 1355 BS vide kabala Ext. 4. The plaintiffs are men of Comilla. They left their home district after the above purchase and remained here for two years. Their case is that in the meantime, Naldanga Raj Estate, the landlord of the suit land, brought a rent suit against them with respect to the suit lands and other lands and auction purchased the same. The plaintiffs deposited the decretal dues vide the chalan Ext. 5 and saved the suit property. The further case of the plaintiffs is that some heirs of Jogeswar Babu and others brought Misc. Case No. 15 of 1955 for setting aside the auction purchase of the suit land by Satyen Babu. The plaintiffs contested that Misc. Case and it was dismissed vide order Ext. 6. After their return from Comilla, the plaintiffs came to learn that defendant No. 1 and Babar Ali, husband of defendant No. 7 are illegally possessing the 'Ka' and 'Kha' schedule land. On query, they disclosed that they took lease of the suit land separately from Ramani Sundari, pro-defendant No. 8 by executing kabuliats vide Ext. 2(1) and 2(b). The plaintiffs came to learn that defendant No. 1 and Babar Ali executed those kabuliats after the sale of the suit land by Ramani Sundari to the plaintiffs in order to deprive the plaintiffs from the suit land. They did not acquire any title in the suit land on the basis of their kabuliat. 

 5. The defence case in short is, that Madhu Mondal and Haran Mondal did not surrender their raiyati interest in the suit land in favour of landlord Jageswar Chattapadhyaya and others. The further case of the defence is that the landlords obtained a kabuliat from Takim Mondal on misrepresentation and Takim Mondal was never put in possession of the land covered by the kabuliat and Haran Mondal all along possessed the land during his life time. The kabuliat executed by Takim Mondal was not acted upon and defendant No. 1, son of Takim Mondal does not claim any interest in the suit land on the basis of that kabuliat. As Madhu Mondal requested the landlords to reduce the rent of Taka 50.00 to Taka 45.00 the landlords agreed to reduce the rent by Taka 5.00, but at the same time, demanded kabuliat. Accordingly, Madhu Mondal executed a kabuliat. But nonetheless, neither Madhu nor Haran Mondal surrendered their original raiyati in favour of the landlords. Haran Mondal all along possessed the land and died leaving widow proforma defendant No. 6 as his only heiress in the land and defendant No. 6 used to possess the land through bargadars. She then sold the suit land along with other lands to defendant No. 2 by registered kabala dated 11.1.56 vide Ext. A. Since that time, the defendant No. 2 is in possession of the suit land through her husband defendant No. 1. The further case of the defence is that Takim Mondal took lease of 3'/2 bighas of land from Madhu about 17/18 years back at a rental of Tk. 4/10 and defendant No. 1 inherited that land from his father. Defendant No. 1 leased out the eastern half of the plot No. 388 to defendant No. 3 and his brother about 10/11 years back, at a rental of Tk. 5.00 and 4 annas and defendant No. 3 and his brothers are in possession of the land since that time. The Chatterjee landlords never made the lands of the jama of Taka 45.00 khas and they never possessed the suit land in khas. The defendants do not know if Sattyendra Banerjee never auction purchased the interest of Cbattapadhyaya landlords. Sattyendra Nath never possessed the suit land. Ramani Sundari Dasi realised rent from Sauraben Nessa (proforma defendant No. 6) with respect to half of the land of the jama of Taka 45.00 and granted her rent receipt. The plaintiffs did not acquire any title in the suit lands of the above jama of Taka 45.00 from Ramani Sundari on the basis of their purchase, if any, and they never possessed the suit land. Defendant No. 1 and others had criminal litigations with the plaintiffs regarding the suit land and the plaintiffs lost in all those cases. They filed Title Suit No. 253/59 in the second Court of Munsif, Jhenidah, against defendant No. 2, wife of defendant No. 1, but they lost in that suit. The defendants did not dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit lands in Aswin 1337 BS or subsequently, as alleged. The plaintiffs have got no title and possession in the suit land. The learned Munsif dismissed the suit. On appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge upheld and confirmed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif. 

 6. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider, the learned Advocate for the appellants has taken me through pleadings, the impugned judgments of the Courts below and the documents and other evidence on record. It is admitted that the suit lands are recorded in the khatian No. 243 vide Ext. 12 of mouza Bathpukuria within Jhenaidah PS in the names of Madhu Mondal, son of Idhu Mondal and Haran Mondal s/o Sultan Mondal in equal half share, at a rental of Taka 45.00 In the remark column it is written“১৮.৬.৪৬. তারিখের কাবুলিয়ত বিভিন্ন স্বত্বে মোট জমা ৫০.০০ টাকা।  The total area of khas land written in Khatian No. 243 vide Ext. 12 is 15.43 acres and there are 2.94 acres of tenanted land also and the tenanted land is recorded in khatian Nos. 244 and 245. It further appears that Bhagati Chandra Chattapadhyaya had a Dar jote and Nasar Mondal a jote and Jageshwar Chattapadhyaya and others were in possession of both the Dar jote and jote as recorded in Ext. 12. 

 7. The plaintiffs' case is that Madhu Mondal and Haran Mondal orally surrendered their raiyati interest recorded in khatian No. 243 vide Ext. 12 in favour of the landlords. This contention of the plaintiffs is found true by the learned Subordinate Judge. The next contention of the plaintiffs is that after surrender, Madhu Mondal and Takim Mondal, sister's husband of Haran Mondal, took lease of the land in khatian No. 243 by executing separate kabuliats vide Exts. 1 and 1(a) dated 17.2.40. In Exts. 1 and 1(a) it is written that Madhu Mondal and Haran Mondal surrendered the land of the jama of Taka 45.00 and the rental of kabuliat Exts. 1 and 1 (a) was Taka 22.50 each. The defence case is that there was no surrender of the original jama of Taka 45.00 by Haran and Madhu and the kabuliat Ext. 1 executed by Takim was obtained from him by false representation by landlords and the kabuliat was not acted upon. The execution of the kabuliat Ext. 1 is thus admitted by the defence. The case of the plaintiffs is that both Takim and Madhu surrendered their lands of the holdings created by Exts. 1 and 1(a) in favour of the Chattapadhya landlords, whose interest was auction purchased by Sattyendra Nath Bandpadhyaya in Rent Execution Case No. 1722 of 1944 brought by the superior landlords. The plaintiffs filed the certified copy of the suit register and execution register of the above rent suit and rent execution case, in order to prove the auction sale. The plaintiffs also filed the sale certificate Ext. 13. Exhibit 13 is, however, damaged and its contents cannot be fully deciphered clearly. The further case of the plaintiffs in that Satyendra Nath Banerjee, the auction purchaser, took delivery of possession in the suit land and possessed the same in khas and then sold the same to Ramani Sundari by kabala Ext 3 dated 23.8.47. From the suit registers Exts. 14 & 15, it appears that superior landlords of the Chatterjees, obtained decree in RS No. 2550/1944 and the holding was sold in Rent Execution Case No. 1722/1945 and the sale was confirmed on 18.2.46 and delivery of the possession in the auction sold land was taken on 25.8.46. The learned Subordinate Judge found certain discrepancies in the dates given in the certified copies of the register Ext. 14 & 15. From the kabala Ext. 3, it appears that Sattyyndra Nath Banerjee sold the auction purchase land to Ramani Sundari Dasi on 23.8.47 and Ramani Sundari in her turn, sold the same to the plaintiffs by the kabala Ext. 4 dated 29.1.49. The learned Subordinate Judge, although made some criticism regarding the documents, but nonetheless, he held that the interest of Chattapadhaya landlords was acquired by the plaintiffs on the basis of Ext. 4 in the manner stated above. 

 8. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, held that the plaintiffs have failed to prove that Madhu and Takim surrendered their raiyati interest created on the basis of Ext. 1 and 1(a). As already stated, the defence case is that Takim did not take any lease by the kabuliat Ext. 1 as alleged by the defence and Mandu took lease of the holding by Ext. 1(a). Then it is to be presumed that the landlords were in possession of the land of the kabuliat Ext. 1, as it is not the defence case that Madhu was in possession of the entire holding of the original jama of Taka 45.00. The learned Subordinate Judge has held that the plaintiffs have failed to prove khas possession in the suit land by Satyendra Nath, the auction purchaser and Ramani Sundari Dasi on the basis of the auction purchase and subsequent purchase by Ramani Sundari and the plaintiffs also failed to prove their own possession in the suitland. It may be pointed out that the learned Subordinate Judge did not discuss as to the nature of the possession of the suit land. In paragraph 2 for the plaint it is stated as follows “উক্ত বাদপুকুরিয়া মোজার জমি বিশেষভাবে উক্ত ৫০.০০ টাকার জমায় অন্তর্ভুক্ত জমি অত্যন্ত অনুর্বর থাকার ও লোকসংখ্যার অল্পতা হেতু অধিকাংশ বৎসরই পতিত থাকিত।” 

 9. It is admitted that the original raiyats Madhu and Haran surrendered the raiyati holdings in favour of the landlords i.e. land of the original holding of Taka 50.00 or Taka 45.00 came to the khas possession of the Chatterjee landlords. Whether they possessed the land by cultivation physically or not, as soon as the holding was surrendered, the possession of the land in law reverted to the khas possession of the landlords. Thus, it cannot be said that the plaintiff failed to prove the khas possession of the suit land by Chatterjee landlords. The next question is whether Chatterjee landlords possessed the land in khas after the second surrender. As defendants say that Takim did not take lease by the kabuliat Ext. 1, we may assume that the Chatterjee landlords continued to be in possession of at least half of the land of the original holding of Taka 45.00. Thus, the learned Subordinate Judge was not justified in saying that the plaintiffs have failed to prove that Chatterjee landlords were in khas possession, in any part of the suit land. The genuineness of the kabuliat Exts. 1 and 1(a) and the auction sale and the subsequent kabalas Exts. 3 and 4, are not disputed. The learned Subordinate Judge is of opinion that as the Plaintiffs failed to prove khas possession of the suit land by Chatterjee landlords, Sattyendar Nath and Ramani Sundari, they did not acquire any khas land by their purchase by Ext. 4. It may be pointed out that although the plaintiffs admitted in paragraphs 9 and 12 of the plaint that defendants are in possession of the suit land since Kartic 1364 BS. The learned Subordinate Judge did not make any discussion about the evidence' of possession of the defendants in the suit land. There is no evidence to show that the defendants were in possession of the suit land prior to Kartic 1364 BS. He definitely found that the "defendants have not been able to prove that defendant No. 2 has acquired any title in the suit land on the basis of his purchase from proforma defendant No. 6 Souraben Nessa by the kabala Ext. X". If this be so, it may be presumed that Chatterjce landlords were in possession in the suit land in khas, as they were the legal owners. The learned Subordinate Judge also did not make any finding that the defendants were in possession of the suit land at that time. Now, if Chatterjee landlords were in legal possession of the suit land at the time of auction sale. Sattyendra Nath Banerjee by his auction purchase on the basis of Exts. 13, 14 and 15 acquired valid title and possession of the suit land. As already stated, auction purchaser Sattyendra Nath Banerjee took delivery of the possession of the suit land on 25.8.46, as it appears from Ext. 15. Ramani Sundari purchased the land from Satteyndra by Ext. 3 and got both title and also legal possession in the suit land. Thus, it is clear that the plaintiffs' above documents have proved that their predecessors Chatterjce landlords auction purchaser Sattyendra Nath Benerjee and his vendee Ramani Sundari also had legal possession in the suit land. Plaintiffs by their purchase from Ramani Sundari Dasi by Ext. 4 are, therefore, supposed to be in the same legal position and possession in the suit land. 

 "Sec. 3. Except as provided in section 4, no person shall, after the fourteenth day of December, 1948, and for so long as this Act remains in force, transfer any quantity of agricultural land in his khas possession which exceeds, in the aggregate, ten standard big has; and whenever the total quantity of such land transferred by such person after the said date amounts to ten standard big has, he shall be debarred from transferring any more such land." 

 22. He pointed out that the defendants created this kabala Ext. A, after they executed the kabuliats Ext. 2(a) and 2(b) dated 14.2.49 in favour of plaintiffs' vendor Ramani Sundari Dasi. It appears that the kabuliat Ext. 2(a) was executed by Mofizuddin Mondal, defendant No. 1 and Ext. 1(b) by Babor Ali, son of Madhu Mondal, the original tenant and husband of defendant No. 7 Sora Khatun in favour of Ramani Sundari Dasi with respect to the suit land, admitting the title and possession of Ramani Sundari in the suit land. Thus the story that Takim Mondal and Madhu Mondal did not surrender their raiyati interest acquired on the basis of Ext. 1-1 (a) in favour of Chatterjee landlords and the Chatterjee landlords had no khas possession in the holding and the auction purchaser Satyendra Nath Banerjee did not acquire any khas land on the basis of his auction purchase by the sale certificate Ext. 13 and Ramani Dasi also did not acquire any khas land on the basis of her purchase from Satyendra by the kabala Ext. 3 and similarly the plaintiffs also did not acquire khas land on the basis of their purchase by the kabala Ext. 4, have got no basis and no leg to stand upon. The finding of the learned Subordinate Judge to the contrary is thus illegal and against the weight of evidence. The learned Advocate, Mr. Nizamuddin Haider submits that the defendants are now estopped from denying the tide of the plaintiffs or their predecessor in the suit land in Exts 2(a) and 2(b) and the statements made in them in view of the fact the documents are relevant and admissible in evidence in this suit under sections 13 and 21 of the Evidence Act. In support of his contention, he referred to and relied on the decisions reported in 19 DLR 176 and 36 DLR at page 81. In the first case, it was observed as follows : 

 "The statement in the kabala that vendor was in khas possession of the plot transferred by it is admissible under section 13 as it is an assertion and not a mere recital. 

 23. The learned Advocate submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in not considering this aspect of the matter and thus his judgment is vitiated by illegality. The learned Subordinate Judge, it is evident, did not consider the legal implication of the kabuliats Ext. 2(a) and 2(b) executed by the defendant No. 1 and husband of defendant No. 7, admitting the title of the plaintiffs vendor Ramani Sundari, even after the purchase of her interest by the plaintiffs by Ext. 4. As already pointed out, the kabuliats Exts. 2(a) and (b) were executed on 14.2.49 in favour of Ramani Sundari Dasi after she sold the suit land to the plaintiff by kabala Ext. 4 dated 29.1.49. Thus, the plea that the plaintiffs did not acquire any khas land in the holding in suit by their purchase does not hold good. The Courts below found that the suit is barred by limitation. Both the Courts below also found that the suit is barred by limitation as the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land within 12 years prior to the filing of the suit. They probably meant that the suit is barred under Article 142 of the Limitation Act. As already stated the term possession has got varied and wide meaning and there are different kinds of possession such as: physical, legal and symbolical and so on and so forth. In Limitation Act, 1963, by Sanjiva Row under Article 142 at page 90 on the basis of some case decision, possession is described as under: Possession :— Possession is not necessarily the same thing as occupation or actual user, possession means the physical possibility of a person dealing with a property as he likes and not mere physical possession. In other words, not merely physical contact but the possibility of the person dealing with a thing exclusively constitutes possession. Where a person has in his own right and not merely as to be able to exclude others from it and has the intention of exercising that power of exclusion, he can be said to be in possession of it. 

 30. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider, the learned Advocate for the appellants, contends that the learned Subordinate Judge was not justified in finding that the suit is bound to fail as the plaintiffs are to prove their possession within 12 years from the date of filing the suit, irrespective of case of the defence on the point of possession. He submits that the defendants are also to prove their case in a civil suit. The contention of the learned Advocate seems to be correct. Because, in a civil suit both parties give their own cases and lead evidence to that effect, if they are to aucceed. They are obliged to prove their own case. It is no doubt true that the plaintiff is to prove his own case, irrespective of the defence case. But at the same time, the plaintiffs success or failure to prove his case also depends on the defence success or failure to prove his case. In the present case, it is clear that the defendants have miserably failed to show that they are in possession of the suit land for more that 12 years and thereby acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession. They also failed to prove that the plaintiff appellants has no possession within 12 years. As already stated, the possession does not mean always the physical and actual possession. It also means the legal and constructive possession. It the present case, the plaintiffs were in legal and constructive possession of the suit land on the basis of the Ext. 4, as Romani Sundari's khas (tenancy) right and interest in the land is admitted by no other than defendant No. 1 (DW 1) and his wife defendant No. 2 in the kabuliats Ext. 1-1(a) and A. In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case and the legal position discuised, I am of the opinion that the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge is vitiated by error of law and also of fact.
